title: U.S. Navy Blockade Cuts Iran Oil Exports by 90% as Washington Escalates Economic War
excerpt: Iran's crude output has plunged to 259,000 barrels per day as the UAE suspends all trade with Tehran and Treasury freezes $500 billion in crypto assets
body:
• Iran's crude oil exports have plummeted nearly 90% in August to 259,000 barrels per day from 2025 levels, according to Kpler data, as the U.S. Navy blockade chokes off Tehran's primary revenue source.
  • The UAE has suspended all trade with Iran, and the U.S. Treasury has sanctioned over 1,000 entities since Trump's second term began, freezing an estimated $500 billion in Iran-linked cryptocurrency.
  • Brent crude has climbed above $94 a barrel amid deepening supply concerns, with shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz falling to a fraction of pre-war levels.

The U.S. Navy's blockade of Iranian ports has slashed Iran's crude oil exports by nearly 90% in August, reducing output to just 259,000 barrels per day from 2025 levels, according to Kpler data — the sharpest sustained decline since the six-month U.S.-Iran conflict began in February.

The figures emerged as President Donald Trump's administration escalated what it has called "economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale," combining the naval embargo with a sweeping new sanctions offensive aimed at severing Iran's remaining economic lifelines.

An Indefinite Blockade

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. military could maintain the naval blockade indefinitely, rotating ships in and out of the region to enforce the embargo on Iranian oil.

"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to."

— Pete Hegseth, U.S. Defense Secretary

The economic pressure deepened when the United Arab Emirates — which accounts for roughly 30% of Iran's imports — suspended all trade activities, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Tehran until further notice. Two vessels from Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz last week, in what the UAE condemned as an Iranian strike.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what he called "the greatest financial offensive ever marshalled," though specifics remained limited. The Treasury Department has sanctioned more than 1,000 people, vessels, and aircraft connected to Iran since Trump began his second term, targeting Iran's shadow oil fleet, shipping insurers, weapons-procurement networks, and digital exchanges. An estimated $500 billion in Iran-linked cryptocurrency has been frozen.

Bessent singled out Iran's Bank Melli, which continues to operate branches across Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. "Every branch of Bank Melli must be shuttered and dark," he said.

Tehran Dismisses the Pressure

Iran has responded with defiance, vowing to shut down all oil exports from the Gulf "if the economic war continues" and warning that ships cannot pass through the Strait of Hormuz without its permission. Iran's Oil Minister insisted that oil sales in "distant waters" have not stopped despite the reduction, according to state media.

But analysts note that Iran's floating oil storage has shrunk to a five-month supply, suggesting the economic damage is deeper than Tehran acknowledges. The Treasury has also targeted independent Chinese refineries that had been purchasing Iranian crude, further reducing demand for embargoed barrels.

Oil Markets Feel the Strain

Brent crude has climbed above $94 a barrel, with traders increasingly concerned that the conflict and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz will not be resolved quickly. Before the war, the strait handled roughly a fifth of the world's daily oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.

Shipping traffic through the waterway has plummeted. On one recent day, just eight vessels transited the strait — compared with 130 to 140 ships daily before the conflict began.

"Hormuz is still a problem, but it is no longer the only story. Pipelines, shuttles, U.S. shale, a recovering Venezuela, and an unconstrained UAE are all adding barrels."

— Phil Flynn, Senior Analyst, Price Futures Group

But the global refining system is under enormous strain. U.S. refineries have operated near maximum capacity for the longest sustained period in over a quarter century, scrambling to meet surging demand for diesel and jet fuel — a pace analysts warn is unsustainable.

What Comes Next

With a tentative June peace deal in tatters and neither side willing to return to negotiations, the standoff appears entrenched. Trump has warned of economic consequences against any country providing "any type of lifeline to Iran," a veiled threat aimed partly at China, historically Iran's largest oil buyer.

For India, the disruption carries direct consequences. Rising crude prices have pressured the rupee and widened the trade deficit, with Brent's climb toward $100 threatening to push inflation higher and squeeze consumer spending across the subcontinent.
nri_angle: Rising crude prices from the Iran blockade are pressuring India's trade deficit and the rupee, directly affecting NRI investments and the cost of living for families in India.
